stories.headline: Update: Oil Prices Plunge as U.S. Officials Signal Imminent Deal to Reopen Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary:
Oil prices fell to three-week lows Tuesday after senior U.S. officials signaled that a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could be reached within days. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said progress had been made in discussions with Iran and Oman, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC there was 'a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow.' Brent crude dropped nearly 5% to under $80 a barrel, and U.S. West Texas Intermediate fell more than 5% to $76.

The Strait of Hormuz has been closed to most traffic since a conflict between the U.S. and Iran began in late February, disrupting roughly one-fifth of global daily oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. Iran has maintained it is not negotiating directly with the United States, saying it is instead working through Omani mediators. A spokesman for Iran's foreign ministry described talks with Oman on a new shipping mechanism as 'positive,' while Qatar said it was continuing diplomatic efforts but acknowledged no direct U.S.-Iran talks were currently planned.

The disclosure added urgency to the geopolitical standoff: CBS News reported, citing two sources with direct knowledge, that the U.S. has used nearly all of its global stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the conflict. A Houthi naval blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports, in place since July 20, has further complicated global shipping routes that had served as an alternative to the closed strait.

Previous rounds of negotiations have repeatedly stalled, leaving energy markets volatile and consumers facing elevated fuel prices. The gap between U.S. claims of progress and Iran's public denials of direct talks means any deal remains uncertain, and analysts cautioned that Tuesday's price drop could reverse quickly if negotiations again collapse.

stories.headline: Trump-Backed John James Wins Michigan GOP Gubernatorial Primary; Several Other Races Decided
stories.summary:
Republican Rep. John James won Michigan's GOP gubernatorial primary Tuesday, defeating multimillionaire businessman Perry Johnson in a race that tested President Trump's endorsement power in a key battleground state. The Associated Press called the race for James, a West Point graduate and Army Ranger who served multiple combat tours in Iraq and was endorsed by Trump in late June. James will face two-term Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson in the general election to succeed term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

The primary turned sharply negative, with Johnson — who is white — calling James, one of the few Black Republicans in Congress, a 'DEI candidate' and accusing him of playing the 'race card' in a recent debate. James called Johnson 'desperate.' Johnson dramatically outspent James with millions of his own money but could not overcome the Trump endorsement advantage. Michigan's governorship is considered a high-stakes and expensive general election contest in a state both parties view as essential.

Primary elections were also held Tuesday in Virginia, Kansas, and Missouri, with results continuing to come in. The Michigan result reinforces Trump's continued influence over Republican primary outcomes heading into the 2026 midterm cycle, though his endorsed candidates have faced mixed results in other contests this cycle.

Democrats will watch the Michigan general election closely. Benson, a well-known statewide figure who successfully defended her secretary of state seat in 2022, enters the race with significant name recognition. The contest is expected to draw national attention and funding from both parties given Michigan's status as a perennial swing state.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Revokes Visa of Brazil's Ambassador in Escalating Diplomatic Dispute
stories.summary:
The Trump administration revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador to the United States, Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti, in what the State Department characterized as a reciprocal response to Brazil's diplomatic actions. The move follows Brazil's denial of visas last month for two American diplomats who sought to visit the country ahead of October elections, as well as Brazil's refusal to approve Trump's ambassadorial nominee, former Florida House Speaker Danny Perez. State Department officials said the step had been delayed multiple times to give Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva an opportunity to back down.

Despite the revocation, Viotti is not being expelled and could resume her duties if Brazil accepts Perez as the U.S. ambassador. Officials indicated Brazil is unlikely to act before its October 4 presidential election, in which Lula will face Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whose family has close ties to the Trump administration. The U.S. had denied any intent to interfere in Brazilian elections, calling a planned trip by Assistant Secretary Riley Barnes 'routine' and focused on election integrity and religious freedom.

The diplomatic rift has deepened across multiple fronts. The Trump administration recently classified Brazil's two largest drug-trafficking organizations as foreign terrorist organizations — a designation Lula opposes — and imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, which took effect Friday. Lula's government views these moves as hostile acts tied to Trump's alignment with the Bolsonaro political family.

The standoff represents one of the more serious bilateral ruptures between the United States and a major Latin American ally in recent years. Brazil is South America's largest economy and a historically significant trading and diplomatic partner for Washington. Both sides have left open the possibility of a rapid reversal if the ambassador dispute is resolved.

stories.headline: OpenAI to Pay $3.2 Million to Settle DOJ Allegations of Discrimination Against U.S. Workers
stories.summary:
OpenAI agreed Tuesday to pay $3.2 million to settle Justice Department allegations that it discriminated against U.S. workers by favoring temporary visa holders in recruiting and hiring. The settlement also covers Statsig, a product development software subsidiary, which the DOJ alleged similarly prioritized foreign workers holding temporary employment visas over qualified American applicants. The Justice Department framed the action as a warning to the broader technology sector.

'It is illegal to discriminate against U.S. workers,' the DOJ stated in announcing the settlement. The Trump administration has made cracking down on companies that use visa programs to bypass American talent a stated enforcement priority, and officials said the fine against one of the world's most prominent artificial intelligence companies was intended to put the tech industry on notice. OpenAI did not immediately admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement.

The case highlights ongoing tension between the technology industry's reliance on skilled foreign workers through programs such as the H-1B visa and the administration's push to prioritize domestic hiring. The AI sector in particular has drawn scrutiny for heavy use of international talent pipelines, even as it has become one of the most economically and strategically significant industries in the United States.

OpenAI is currently one of the most closely watched companies in the world, having recently gone public and operating at the center of a global race in artificial intelligence development. The settlement adds a regulatory and reputational dimension to the company's challenges as it navigates rapid growth, increasing competition, and heightened government attention.

stories.headline: Update: Houthi Projectile Sinks Indian-Flagged Ship Off Yemen Coast as Red Sea Attacks Escalate
stories.summary:
An Indian-flagged vessel, the MSV Faize Noore Oliya, capsized and sank after being struck by a projectile off the coast of Yemen, India's Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal confirmed Tuesday. All 14 people aboard were safely rescued, including 13 Indian nationals. Yemen's internationally recognized transportation ministry accused Iran-backed Houthi fighters of carrying out the attack using an explosives-laden boat.

The sinking is the latest in a series of attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea, a route that gained importance after Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports on July 20, and UK maritime authorities have logged several attacks on vessels in the region over the past week.

India's Ministry of External Affairs called the attacks on commercial shipping "deeply worrisome" and demanded that "free and unimpeded navigation through international waterways be restored at the earliest." The Houthi group has not commented on the incident.

Despite the escalating shipping dangers, oil prices fell to a three-week low Tuesday after senior U.S. officials signaled progress toward a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested an agreement could come as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday, though Iran has publicly stated it is not negotiating directly with the United States and is instead engaging through Oman.

stories.headline: Mass Funeral Held in Gaza for 112 Palestinians Killed in 2023 Israeli Strike, Bodies Newly Recovered from Rubble
stories.summary:
Large crowds gathered in Gaza City Tuesday for a mass funeral for 112 people — mostly women and children — killed in an Israeli airstrike on a residential block in the Sabra neighborhood on November 22, 2023, early in the Gaza war. The victims, members of the Abu Sharia and Hassayna extended families, had only recently been recovered from under rubble in a two-week excavation operation supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross. Among the dead were 44 children, 38 women, and seven people with disabilities.

Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal said the multi-storey building had been leveled with more than 180 civilians inside, estimating roughly 90 percent were killed. The BBC has requested information from the Israel Defense Forces on what was targeted but had not received a response at the time of publication. The funeral is described as the largest of its kind held in Gaza since the war began.

The recovery effort was carried out by Gaza's Civil Defence with ICRC logistical and training support, including excavators, body bags, and protective equipment. ICRC spokesperson Patrick Griffiths said the confirmation of death, while painful, was essential for families seeking closure.

Since the start of the war — triggered by the Hamas-led assault on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people and took 251 hostage — at least 73,377 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, figures the UN considers broadly reliable.

stories.headline: Salmonella Outbreak Prompts Chipotle to Pull Jalapeños from Restaurants Across Multiple States
stories.summary:
Chipotle Mexican Grill announced Tuesday it has voluntarily removed jalapeños from an undisclosed number of its restaurants after public health authorities launched an investigation into a salmonella outbreak linked to several Mexican-style quick-service restaurants. The Minnesota Department of Health has identified 110 illnesses, with many patients reporting they ate at Chipotle between mid-June and mid-July. Investigators cautioned that not every illness has been directly linked to the chain and that other restaurants may have received the contaminated ingredient.

Chipotle said it traced jalapeños as a potential common ingredient from a shared lot and replaced them with product from different growers. The company did not disclose how many locations were affected or identify the original supplier. The Food and Drug Administration has launched a traceback investigation focused on jalapeños and other possible ingredients.

Minnesota health officials said they no longer believe the peppers pose an ongoing risk at Chipotle locations, as the suspected product has been removed, but warned the outbreak could continue if contaminated jalapeños remain in circulation at other food service establishments. The Houthi Houthis have not commented.

stories.headline: FBI Supervisory Agent Charged After Stealing Nearly $1 Million in Cryptocurrency Seized from Criminal Targets
stories.summary:
A supervisory FBI special agent, Patrick Steven Yaroch, was arrested and faces two federal charges after allegedly transferring more than $900,000 in cryptocurrency from accounts tied to foreign criminal targets into his personal wallet, the Justice Department announced. Yaroch was fired by the FBI last week before his arrest on charges of interstate transportation of stolen goods and receipt of stolen goods.

In an affidavit, Yaroch admitted to the transfers but reportedly told investigators he believed the FBI "could not or would not act" against the adversarial cryptocurrency accounts linked to overseas criminal operations. Prosecutors did not accept that justification as a defense.

The case represents a significant breach of trust within federal law enforcement, involving a senior agent exploiting access to seized digital assets. Three outlets — CBS News, NBC Politics, and The Hill — are covering the arrest.

stories.headline: Officials Confirm Southern California Edison Equipment Caused Deadly 2025 Eaton Fire
stories.summary:
Los Angeles County Fire officials released a report Tuesday formally blaming Southern California Edison equipment for the Eaton Fire, which killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses in January 2025. Investigators concluded that electrical arcing events on an out-of-service SCE tower ignited dry brush below, with two arcing events occurring in quick succession and sparking a blaze that spread within seconds across the San Gabriel Mountains, Altadena, Pasadena, Sierra Madre, and La Cañada Flintridge.

The investigation was conducted jointly by the Los Angeles County Arson Fire Investigation Unit and Cal Fire over 18 months, using electrical and metallurgical experts. Officials found SCE was responsible for maintaining and operating its lines and equipment in a manner that minimized wildfire risk. The utility had previously acknowledged its equipment was likely associated with the fire's ignition.

SCE spokesperson Kathleen Dunleavy said the company has received the report and is reviewing it, adding that SCE has 'taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the very beginning.' In ongoing litigation, SCE has claimed Los Angeles County agencies failed to issue timely evacuation warnings and that water agencies did not provide adequate water for firefighting — allegations Los Angeles County declined to address in response to this report.

The official determination carries major legal and financial implications for the utility, which faces numerous civil suits from victims and their families. Eighteen of the 19 people who died in the fire lived in west Altadena. The fire took nearly a month to fully extinguish and scorched 22 square miles.

stories.headline: Record 173 Migrants Rescued After English Channel Boat Fire; UK Says All Will Be Returned to France
stories.summary:
More than 170 migrants were rescued Tuesday after the boat they were using to cross the English Channel from France caught fire, the French maritime prefecture confirmed. The vessel, carrying 173 people — breaking the previous record of 165 for the largest single migrant boat to attempt the crossing — had its engine ignite, causing the structure to deteriorate rapidly. All survivors were taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer in France, with 11 suffering minor injuries. French prosecutors opened an investigation and an Egyptian national was taken into custody in connection with the incident.

The boat had left France on Monday night. French authorities said five people initially required rescue but the remaining passengers refused assistance from French patrol boats, determined to reach the UK. Only when the fire caused the vessel's structural integrity to fail rapidly did the migrants accept help. Rescue operations involved 40 firefighters, 13 police officers, seven interpreters, British Border Force vessels, and the RNLI Eastbourne lifeboat.

UK Border Security Minister Anna Turley said the incident 'shows the dangers of these illegal crossings and the ruthless gangs behind them,' adding the government is 'bearing down on them.' A UK government spokesperson said all rescued migrants 'will be returned' to France and that British vessels had assisted in the operation. No fatalities were reported.

Between January 1 and August 3 of this year, 14,561 people have crossed the Channel by small boat from France. The record vessel size underscores continued pressure on both the UK and French governments over Channel migration policy, a politically charged issue in both countries.

stories.headline: Cameroon's Absent 93-Year-Old President Reshuffles Military From Geneva After Two Months Away
stories.summary:
Cameroonian President Paul Biya, who has not been seen publicly in nearly two months, issued military reshuffling decrees Monday from Geneva, where he has been staying since leaving Cameroon on June 7. The 93-year-old, the world's oldest sitting head of state, appointed officials to key army positions and promoted five colonels to brigadier general, including the reappointment of the commander of the elite presidential guard.

Biya's government has described his stay in Switzerland as a 'brief private stay,' but the prolonged absence — now approaching 60 days — has fueled speculation about his health and generated significant domestic and international concern. The government has denied reports that he is hospitalized, and Cameroon's Communication Minister René Emmanuel Sadi said in a recent interview that Biya is alive and will return soon. Cameroonian media are legally barred from reporting on Biya's health, a restriction condemned by press freedom groups.

The opposition has sharply criticized the situation. CRM party vice-president Mamadou Mota called Biya's absence a 'glaring institutional vacuum,' saying executive power 'is exercised at the heart of the nation, not through smoke signals or telepathy from hotel suites on the other side of the world.' A new vice-presidential post created in April remains unfilled, and a promised new cabinet has not been named.

The military reshuffle follows a pattern under Biya's nearly four-decade rule of using such appointments to signal control during periods of political uncertainty. Analysts note the move echoes reshuffles after the 2023 coup in neighboring Gabon, which toppled a long-ruling dynasty, and during Biya's controversial re-election campaign last year.

stories.headline: Soldier Kills Four in Shooting Rampage in Russian-Occupied Crimea
stories.summary:
A Russian soldier killed four people — including three civilians — in an apparently random gun attack in Russian-annexed Crimea, according to Moscow-installed regional governor Mikhail Razvozhayev. The gunman first opened fire on fellow soldiers, killing one and wounding another, before fatally shooting two elderly men and a 64-year-old woman in the village of Khmelnytske. Three additional people were injured.

The attacker was detained, and authorities said an investigation into the motive was underway. The suspect has not been publicly identified, and officials have not disclosed which branch of the Russian armed forces he served in. Razvozhayev urged residents not to 'spread unverified rumours' about the motive or the attacker's identity.

Russia has controlled Ukraine's Crimean Peninsula since its 2014 annexation, which the vast majority of the international community regards as an illegal occupation of Ukrainian territory. Russia maintains a large military presence in Crimea, which Ukraine has targeted with drone and missile strikes throughout the ongoing war.

The incident adds to a series of violent episodes inside Russian-controlled territory, coming amid an already volatile security environment. It was unclear whether the death toll could rise, with Razvozhayev saying doctors were working to save the injured.

stories.headline: Landslide Kills 14 at Ethiopian Mountain Monastery During Overnight Prayer Service
stories.summary:
A landslide struck an Orthodox Christian monastery in Ethiopia's northern Amhara region in the early hours of Monday morning, killing at least 14 people and injuring seven others, five of them seriously. The hillside above the Tsadqane Debre Mitmaq St Mary Monastery collapsed during heavy overnight rains, burying a prayer chamber carved into the mountainside where worshippers had gathered for a holy water cleansing ritual.

Local official Dagnachew Azbite told the BBC that the land above the cave slid following sustained heavy rainfall throughout the night. Many of the victims had gathered to receive holy water, a practice popular among Ethiopian Orthodox Christians seeking healing for chronic illnesses. Rescue operations have since been halted, and funerals have been held for several of the deceased at the monastery itself.

The disaster adds to a pattern of deadly landslides and floods in Ethiopia during the annual rainy season, which runs from June to August. A landslide in the neighboring Geze Gofa Zone killed more than 229 people in July 2024, and flooding in southern Ethiopia's Gamo Zone killed more than 100 earlier this year. Scientists have warned that climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of extreme rainfall events across East Africa.

stories.headline: SpaceX Falcon 9 Rocket Stage on Collision Course With Moon, Impact Expected Wednesday
stories.summary:
The upper stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket is expected to collide with the Moon on Wednesday, August 5, at approximately 2:35 a.m. EDT, according to NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies. The roughly 4,000-kilogram section — about the size of a five-story building — has been drifting since a January 2025 mission that carried lunar landers and scientific equipment, and was independently identified by astronomers using public tracking data.

The impact is predicted to occur near the Einstein Crater on the visible, sunlit side of the Moon, traveling at approximately 5,400 miles per hour. Astronomer Bill Gray, who first identified the trajectory, estimates the collision will create a crater more than 17 meters in diameter and send a plume of debris an estimated 50 kilometers into space. NASA has said there is no danger to Earth and plans to observe the impact site for scientific purposes.

The event underscores growing concerns about space debris as commercial launch activity accelerates. Unlike reusable first-stage boosters, upper stages are shed in space and can remain in unstable orbits for years. Astronomers say the impact, while not visible to the naked eye, may produce a detectable flash for those with sophisticated telescopes.

stories.headline: France Wildfires Unearth Cache of 400 World War II Shells in Gironde Village
stories.summary:
Wildfires that burned through the Gironde region of southwestern France revealed a cache of approximately 400 historic munitions — including German and French mortar and anti-tank shells — buried beneath the village of Le Porge, local authorities announced Monday. More than 100 explosions heard during the second night of the fire, initially attributed to gas cylinders, are now believed to have been World War II-era explosives detonated by the heat, according to the local fire commander.

Le Porge's mayor, Martial Zaninetti, described the blasts as sounding "like the sound of war," with shells flying in multiple directions and one passing through a house. Demining operations have allowed most residents to return home, though the mayor said certain areas — including access to the ocean, a campsite, and the nearby village of La Jenny — remain off-limits. More than 180 homes in the area were destroyed by the wildfire.

The Gironde fire was among the most destructive in a broader wave of wildfires that swept across Europe over the past two weeks, burning approximately 42,000 hectares in southwestern France in what French officials described as one of the largest forest fires since World War II. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday thanked firefighters and said the crisis had entered a "new phase" as evacuated residents began returning home.

stories.headline: Update: Ceuta Migrant Crisis — Morocco Blames Misinformation as Spain Says Nearly All Have Left
stories.summary:
Morocco's government blamed misinformation and human trafficking networks for luring tens of thousands of migrants into illegally crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta last week, pushing back against criticism of Rabat's border management. A Moroccan minister told reporters at least 75 people died in connection with the crossings as EU foreign ministers met to discuss the bloc's response to the crisis.

Spain's foreign minister said nearly all of the roughly 50,000 undocumented migrants who crossed into Ceuta have now left, seeking to reassure European partners that Madrid is swiftly returning arrivals. Italy moved to suspend border-free travel with Spain in a step analysts called more political than practical, while the EU faced accusations that its panic was emboldening smugglers and far-right parties across the continent.

The crisis has exposed deep fault lines within the European Union over migration burden-sharing. Spain's far-right Vox party called the crossings an 'invasion' and blamed the government, while critics of the hard right argued that inflammatory rhetoric strengthened smuggling networks. EU officials called for emergency coordination to prevent a repeat.

Spain had urgently requested an emergency meeting of EU ministers, which has now taken place. The episode underscores the strategic vulnerability of European enclaves in North Africa and the difficulty of coordinating a continental response to sudden large-scale migration events.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Strikes Moscow-Region Warehouse, Killing Five; Russia Hits Ukrainian Cities
stories.summary:
Ukrainian drone strikes overnight killed at least five people and injured ten at an industrial warehouse site about 69 kilometers south of Moscow, local Russian officials said Tuesday. The site in Chekhov was reported by Ukrainian media and listed on Yandex as a Wildberries facility, though Russian authorities did not formally confirm the connection. Separately confirmed Wildberries sites in the St. Petersburg and Tver regions were also struck, and a Samara warehouse hit Sunday was described as completely destroyed.

Kyiv has been systematically targeting Wildberries warehouses — Russia's largest online retailer, sometimes called the 'Russian Amazon' — claiming the depots supply the Russian military. Moscow denies the facilities have any military function. Russia's defense ministry said it intercepted and destroyed 320 drones overnight, one of the higher figures claimed in a single night since the war began.

Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least four people overnight. An 89-year-old woman was killed and two young girls injured in a strike on Mykolaiv, while a woman and two girls aged five and ten were killed in a residential strike on Sumy. A food warehouse in Dnipro was set ablaze and two people were injured in Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi.

The exchange of strikes comes a day after a Ukrainian drone hit a crowded beach in Russia's Krasnodar region, killing seven people and injuring 58. Ukrainian Telegram channels suggested the drone struck the beach after electronic warfare jammed its navigation signal, a claim Russian authorities have not confirmed.

stories.headline: Fuego Volcano Erupts in Guatemala, Forcing Evacuations Near Antigua
stories.summary:
Guatemala's Fuego volcano, one of the most active in the Western Hemisphere, began erupting Monday, sending lava and ash into the air and forcing the evacuation of at least two villages on its slopes. Pyroclastic currents — fast-moving rivers of gas, ash, and rock — continued flowing down the volcano's southeastern flank into Tuesday morning, according to the government monitoring agency.

Guatemala's disaster management agency Conred issued a nationwide orange alert, the second-highest level, and urged residents near the volcano to keep windows and doors closed. Schools in surrounding areas canceled classes. Officials warned that further eruptions could produce additional pyroclastic flows and ash clouds.

Fuego is located just 16 kilometers from Antigua, a UNESCO World Heritage city popular with tourists for its colonial architecture, and has also become a destination for hikers. Authorities urged visitors and residents to avoid the volcano's slopes and surrounding risk zones.

The eruption carries echoes of a 2018 disaster at Fuego when more than 200 people were killed, many caught by fast-moving pyroclastic flows in the Las Lajas ravine. No deaths have been reported in the current eruption.

stories.headline: Three Polls Show Democrat Talarico Narrowly Leading Paxton in Texas Senate Race
stories.summary:
Democrat James Talarico holds a slim two-point lead over Republican Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, in the state's U.S. Senate race, according to a new poll from the Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center at Texas Southern University. The survey found Talarico at 47 percent to Paxton's 45 percent, within the margin of error. It is the third consecutive poll to show Talarico ahead in what is shaping up as one of the most closely watched Senate contests of the 2026 cycle.

Republican strategists have not publicly sounded alarms, but the internal theory among Paxton's camp acknowledges troubling trends among white and Latino voters in a state that has not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988. Democrats view a Texas pickup as critical to their Senate majority hopes, and Talarico has focused his campaign on winning back male voters who have drifted toward Republicans.

Paxton, a two-term attorney general, survived a 2022 impeachment effort by the Texas House and has remained a polarizing figure even within Republican circles. Democrats are framing Paxton's legal controversies as a liability, while Republicans argue that Texas's structural lean will ultimately carry their nominee across the finish line.

The race has drawn national money and attention from both parties. The outcome could be decisive in determining which party controls the Senate, making Texas a central battleground as the midterm election approaches.

stories.headline: Update: Arson Suspect Arrested as Spokane Wildfires Destroy 700 Structures, Force 67,000 Evacuations
stories.summary:
Authorities arrested 37-year-old Aaron F. Farinacci on Monday on suspicion of arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire, one of several blazes burning around Spokane, Washington. He is being held on $1 million bond, and it was not immediately clear if he had legal representation. The fires together have destroyed at least 700 structures and forced roughly 67,000 residents to evacuate, making them among the most destructive blazes in state history.

Residents returning to their neighborhoods Monday found homes leveled to their foundations, with only chimneys remaining in some cases. The fires have burned approximately 12.5 square miles across eastern Washington, jumping roads and rivers. Calmer winds and lower temperatures provided some relief to firefighters Monday, though hot and dry conditions were expected to return by midweek.

Washington's governor spoke directly with President Trump about the disaster. The arrest of a suspected arsonist adds a criminal dimension to a disaster that was already straining state emergency resources and drawing national attention.

stories.headline: Update: Blanche AG Nomination Clears Path as Cornyn and Tillis Back Confirmation After Fund Rescission
stories.summary:
Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina announced Monday they will support acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination to permanently lead the Justice Department, ending a standoff that had threatened to block the confirmation. The two senators had withheld support until they received written confirmation that the administration's proposed $1.8 billion 'Anti-Weaponization Fund' was formally dead. Blanche issued a written order late Sunday declaring unequivocally that 'there is no Fund,' paving the way for the Senate Judiciary Committee to advance his nomination Tuesday.

The fund, proposed as part of a settlement of President Trump's lawsuit against the IRS, had drawn bipartisan criticism over concerns that violent participants in the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot could qualify for payments. Cornyn and Tillis also pressed the Justice Department to narrow the scope of a separate provision granting broad immunity from tax audits to Trump and members of his family.

Separately, the Justice Department on Monday moved to dismiss a class action lawsuit filed by January 6 defendants under the Federal Tort Claims Act, arguing the claims were filed well past the two-year statute of limitations. Critics of the Blanche order noted it contains no explicit language barring future government payouts to convicted rioters, and a former DOJ lawyer argued the unilateral rescission has no permanent legal effect.

stories.headline: Michigan Senate Democratic Primary Pits Establishment Against Progressive Wing on Eve of Vote
stories.summary:
Michigan Democrats head to the polls Tuesday in a closely watched Senate primary that has become a proxy battle over the future direction of the party. Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who flipped a Republican district in 2018 and served in the Obama administration's auto industry rescue, is running against Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive physician and former public health director who has never held elected office. Recent polling shows the race effectively tied.

Stevens's supporters argue she is best positioned to win a general election in a purple state, pointing to her record and cross-partisan appeal. El-Sayed's backers contend the party needs an authentic, uncompromising progressive voice to motivate new voters. Right-leaning outlets have highlighted a 2018 video in which El-Sayed argued that denying driver's licenses to undocumented immigrants amounted to discrimination — a position likely to feature prominently in Republican attacks if he wins the nomination.

The race carries significant national implications. Michigan is a key swing state, and the seat is seen as a potential pickup opportunity for Democrats as they seek to build a Senate majority. The primary result will signal whether Democratic base voters in competitive states are moving toward pragmatic electability arguments or progressive mobilization strategies heading into November.

stories.headline: Iranian Cyberattack Suspected in Coordinated Strikes on Water Systems Across Seven U.S. States
stories.summary:
The FBI has warned that cyberattacks on water infrastructure have been reported in seven U.S. states, with some attacks degrading actual water operations. The incidents began with Minnesota reporting that more than 30 of its water systems had been subjected to a coordinated cyberattack. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is investigating a possible Iranian connection, though it has declined to comment publicly.

Cyber experts told the BBC the attacks bear hallmarks of Iranian state-linked activity, noting that a group called Handala — which the Justice Department has linked to Iran — has carried out most Iranian cyberattacks against U.S. and Israeli targets this year. Investigators are also examining whether the attackers may have posed as Iranian operatives as a disinformation ruse. Iran has not commented on the current incidents and has historically denied involvement in previous cyberattacks attributed to it.

President Trump blamed 'grossly incompetent' Minnesota officials, including Democratic Governor Tim Walz, at a cabinet meeting Friday. Walz responded that Trump 'knows exactly who is responsible for this attack.' Analysts noted the Trump administration may face political pressure not to publicly confirm Iranian involvement given its ongoing broader conflict with Tehran, even if attribution is established.
